title: Principles: The Secret of Athleticism
tagline: Why elite movers look effortless, and what Coach Chong Xie's foot-to-glute philosophy teaches the rest of us.
intro_markdown:
Watch a great athlete move and you notice something that has nothing to do with muscle size. They look light, springy, connected and *calm*. Their power seems to come from nowhere.

This module is built on the work of **Coach Chong Xie**, founder of **Secret of Athleticism** and creator of **Hyperarch Fascia Training (HFT)**. His YouTube channel, titled *Coach Chong Xie* (handle **@HyperarchFasciaTraining**), is built around one core idea: elite athletes are not just stronger. They are *connected differently* from the feet up, through their fascia.

Over five lessons you will learn:

1. **Who Chong Xie is** and how he arrived at his "secret"
2. **The foot-to-glute connection**, the centre of his whole system
3. **The spectrum of athleticism**, from muscle-driven to fascia-driven
4. **Where gym culture goes wrong**, and where it still has a place
5. **The Basic Three**, his starter routine you can do at home today

A note on honesty. Chong Xie is a coach and practitioner, and many of his ideas are his own observations and hypotheses. Where mainstream research backs him up, we show you the study. Where it doesn't yet, we say so. And there is real news here: in October 2026 the first randomized trial of his method was published in a peer-reviewed journal. You will see exactly what it found.

Josh's own conviction, that a healthy fascial system is what has kept him off the physio table since around 2021-22 after years of chronic injury, is presented for what it is: lived experience, and the reason this course exists. Bold ideas, honestly sourced.

lessons.title: Meet the Source: Chong Xie and the Secret of Athleticism
lessons.summary: The coach behind 'Secret of Athleticism' noticed that elite athletes used their feet completely differently from everyone else in the gym. That observation became a training system, a philosophy, and now a published clinical trial.
lessons.body_markdown:
## A coach who started by looking down

Most coaches study what athletes lift. Chong Xie started by studying how they *stand*.

In a short clip on his channel, *The difference between PRO's and YOU*, he tells the origin story. Training barefoot alongside highly athletic people, squatting and deadlifting, he noticed their feet behaved differently from his. Their toes gripped. Their tendons stood out. His feet just sat there while he moved the weight.

The second clue came from EMG (electrical muscle activity) testing. According to Xie, when elite athletes simply stood and began to walk, their glutes were already switched on. In most people, including himself back then, the glutes stayed quiet and the quads did the work. His conclusion: the difference was not strength. It was a neurological connection, built through how those athletes had developed their feet.

That one idea, that elite athleticism starts in the feet and travels through the fascia to the glutes, is the seed of everything in this module.

## Who is Chong Xie?

Here is what we could verify:

- He founded **Secret of Athleticism**, which began as a website and discussion group dedicated to understanding the foot. The site's banner says it has been "disrupting the health and fitness world since 2013" with original work on what he calls the **Hyperarch mechanism**.
- He created **Hyperarch Fascia Training (HFT)**, which he says draws on Chinese martial arts principles combined with current research on fascia.
- He came from tech, not sport. The Just Fly Performance podcast introduced him as having a computer science degree and about ten years as a technical analyst in the software industry.
- On his own website he says he once believed elite athletes succeeded mainly through genetics and natural talent, and that roughly a decade of research and experimentation changed his mind.
- He has worked with elite athletes. UFC champion **Zhang Weili** lists him as her Hyperarch Fascia Training coach. He has also hosted a joint webinar with one of the world's best-known fascia researchers, **Dr. Robert Schleip**, and says he has taken part in fascia dissection at Stanford.

You may hear his name spelled or pronounced a few different ways. The correct spelling is **Chong Xie**.

## The core belief: it's not what they do, it's how they do it

This sums up his philosophy. In his *Crash Course*, Xie argues that the "naturals" you see on TV were not made in the weight room. Their fascial connections were built young, through how they used their bodies. So two people can do the exact same exercise and get completely different results, because the internal foundation is different.

He uses a computer analogy, which makes sense given his background:

- **Hardware** is the visible structure: the shape of the foot, the prominent tendons, the calf.
- **Software** is the internal foundation: how force and signals travel through the fascial web.

Mainstream training, in his view, mostly upgrades the muscles. HFT tries to upgrade the connection.

## You are not stuck with what you were born with

This is the most hopeful part of the message. If athleticism were purely genetic, there would be nothing to train. Xie's own journey, from believing in talent to believing in development, says otherwise. In his view, most people who grew up in cushioned shoes are not unathletic. They are under-connected, and connection can be rebuilt.

This is exactly where Josh's story fits. Years of chronic injuries. Money spent on physio. Feeling lost. Then a shift to simple, at-home fascial work, and no physio visit since around 2021-22, despite training harder than ever. That is not a clinical trial. It is one person's lived proof, and it is why this course exists.

## What the evidence says

Be clear-eyed here. It makes you a smarter student.

- Many of Xie's ideas are **his own observations and hypotheses**, developed through coaching.
- Several of his foundations line up with mainstream fascia research. You will meet those studies in the next lessons.
- His method has now been **formally tested**. In October 2026, the journal *Sports* published a randomized controlled trial run by the Applied Science & Performance Institute (registered as NCT06959472). Physically active adults with chronic ankle instability did 12 weeks of barefoot HFT, about three hours a week, or carried on as normal.

The results were striking. The HFT group reported significantly greater improvement in ankle stability than the control group. Their countermovement jump height rose by about 15 cm on average (roughly 46%), against about 6.6 cm (roughly 19%) in the control group, a statistically significant difference. And this was with no heavy loaded lifts in the programme.

Now the fine print, because you deserve it. Half of the HFT group dropped out, compared with one person in the control group, so the people who finished may have been the most motivated. The study was funded by Hyperarch Fascia Training, and Xie was a co-author (he was not involved in data collection or analysis). Participants were not blinded. Three people in the HFT group stopped because of moderate problems such as increased ankle instability or knee pain, all during unsupervised sessions. One questionnaire, the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure, showed no difference between groups.

So here is the honest picture: a bold practitioner, a growing body of supporting fascia science, and a first trial with exciting results that now needs independent replication.

## Your takeaway

Before you change a single exercise, change the question you ask. Not "how much can I lift?" but **"how connected am I?"** That question is the secret this module is named after.
key_takeaways: Chong Xie founded Secret of Athleticism (his site says 'since 2013') and created Hyperarch Fascia Training (HFT).
His system began with an observation: elite athletes use their feet differently, and their glutes are active even when they simply stand and walk.
His core belief: elite results come from how athletes move, not just what exercises they do. Fascial connection is the 'software' under the visible 'hardware'.
He moved from believing athleticism was mostly genetic to believing it is largely developmental, and can be rebuilt.
The first randomized trial of HFT (Sports, 2026) found significant gains in ankle stability and jump height, with real caveats: 50% dropout in the HFT group, company funding, and no blinding.

lessons.title: From the Ground Up: The Foot-to-Glute Connection
lessons.summary: The centre of Chong Xie's system is a simple idea: tension in the foot switches on the glutes. Here is what he means, what to look for, and the anatomy that supports it.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Your feet are not a flat platform

Chong Xie's message about the foot is blunt: it is not a flat, passive platform.

Most of us, he says, let our feet sit relaxed and flat inside our shoes, putting very little active force into the ground. Elite athletes hold tension in the foot. In his view, if your feet are relaxed, you are not putting enough force into the ground, no matter how strong the rest of your body is. One of his videos is titled exactly around this idea: how much fascial tension in your foot influences your ability to deliver and absorb ground force.

This is the foundation of the **Hyperarch mechanism**: a tensioned, active foot that grips, springs and transmits force upward, instead of a passive foot that simply absorbs impact.

## Why curl the toes?

In a clip analysing LeBron James' feet, Xie explains the purpose of the toe curl. With straight, relaxed toes, the whole foot slaps into the floor. Curl the toes slightly and you pull tension back through the foot and bring the **ball of the foot** into firm contact with the ground. Watch closely and the tendons on top of the foot pop up.

Two key details:

- It is not about curling as hard as you can. If the toes take all the weight, you have gone too far.
- The tension is held *through* the movement. You don't switch it on in mid-air. You leave the ground with it and you land with it.

## The signs of an "elite natural"

In his *Crash Course*, Xie lists the visible signs he associates with a fascially well-developed foot and leg:

- a **prominent anterior tibial tendon** at the front of the ankle
- **visible extensor tendons** on top of the foot
- a **double calf** shape, where the gastrocnemius and soleus are both defined
- a **natural heel suspension** when running, where the heel stays slightly off the ground without straining the calf

He describes being fascia-driven as feeling **lighter**: the heels suspended by the tension network, ground force spread through the whole body, and transitions between movements easier.

Treat these as a coach's observation checklist, not a medical test. They are patterns he has seen in the athletes he studies.

## Foot tension, glute power

Here is the big claim: **the glutes are switched on from the feet.**

In an EMG demonstration on his channel, Xie stands still, no exercise, and shows activity in his gluteus maximus rising simply from tension applied through his feet. In his view, average people lean on the quads and lower back, while elite athletes recruit the core and glutes for the same task.

Why would the foot affect the glutes? Here fascial anatomy gives him real support.

- **The glute is a fascial muscle.** In a 2013 dissection study, **Antonio Stecco, Carla Stecco** and colleagues found that in all six cadavers examined, the gluteus maximus had a major insertion into the **fascia lata**, the fascial sleeve of the thigh. It was so large that the iliotibial tract "could be considered a tendon of insertion of the gluteus maximus." The authors suggest this could explain how force travels from the low back fascia down to the knee. That is very different from the textbook picture of a glute that simply attaches to the thigh bone, and it is exactly the kind of anatomy Xie argues the textbooks underplay.
- **The back of the body is one continuous line.** A 2016 systematic review led by **Jan Wilke** checked Thomas Myers' proposed myofascial chains against dissection studies. It found strong evidence for the **superficial back line**, which runs from the sole of the foot up through the calf and hamstrings to the pelvis and spine, and for the **back functional line**, which links the glute through the fascia to the thigh. The authors concluded that "most skeletal muscles of the human body are directly linked by connective tissue." (Honesty point: the same review found no evidence for Myers' superficial front line. Not every proposed chain holds up.)

So the anatomy is there: continuous connective tissue running from the foot, up the back of the leg, into the pelvis and the glute's fascial attachments. What research has not yet shown is exactly how much foot tension changes glute output in sport. Emerging research suggests these links are functional, and Xie's coaching is built on the bet that they are.

## The foot core

Xie is not alone in saying the foot has been neglected. In a 2015 paper in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine*, Patrick McKeon, Jay Hertel, Dennis Bramble and Irene Davis proposed the **"foot core"** concept. They wrote that the foot's intrinsic muscles "are largely ignored by clinicians and researchers," and that treatment is more often aimed at supporting the foot externally than at training these muscles to function as designed.

That is remarkably close to Xie's critique of cushioned shoes and orthotics, and it comes straight from mainstream sports medicine.

## Babies already know this

One image Xie returns to: look at a baby's feet. Every toe joint moves. Babies grip hard with hands and feet. Over years in comfortable shoes, he argues, we tell the foot it no longer needs to work, and the tissue adapts. The body is efficient. What you don't use, it stops investing in.

## Try this now

Stand barefoot. Lift your heels slightly. Gently curl your toes until the ball of your foot presses firmly into the floor. Hold for 20 seconds and notice where you feel it: only in the foot, in the calf, or all the way up into your glutes?

According to Xie, people with well-connected glutes feel it in the glutes. People without that connection feel it mainly in the foot. Wherever you feel it, that is your starting point.
key_takeaways: Xie's Hyperarch mechanism: an active, tensioned foot that drives force into the ground, instead of a flat, relaxed foot.
A slight toe curl brings the ball of the foot into firm contact and creates tension. Hold it through take-off and landing.
His 'elite natural' signs include a prominent anterior tibial tendon, visible extensor tendons, a double calf and natural heel suspension.
Dissection research shows the gluteus maximus inserts heavily into the fascia lata (Stecco 2013), and a 2016 review confirmed continuous back-of-body chains from the sole of the foot upward.
Mainstream foot researchers also argue the foot's intrinsic muscles are neglected (the 'foot core' paradigm, 2015).

lessons.title: Muscle-Driven vs Fascia-Driven: The Spectrum of Athleticism
lessons.summary: Chong Xie places every athlete on a spectrum, from quad-dominant and muscle-driven to glute-dominant and fascia-driven. Learn where elasticity, stiffness and 'effortless' movement fit in.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Everyone sits somewhere on the spectrum

One of Chong Xie's most useful ideas is that athleticism is not yes-or-no. It is a **spectrum**.

At one end is the **muscle-driven, quad-dominant** mover. At the other is the **fascia-driven, glute-dominant** mover. In part four of his *Crash Course* he makes the point that anyone can be placed somewhere along this line, and no two people sit in exactly the same spot.

At the top end, he says, you see common patterns:

- **higher ankle stiffness**
- **less ankle collapse** (a smaller dorsiflexion angle under load)
- **higher functional stiffness** from better integration
- and, of course, **glute dominance**

This gives you a map. Instead of asking "am I athletic?" you ask "where am I on the spectrum, and which way am I heading?"

## The heel tells the story

In his *Hyperarch Metamorphosis* video, Xie points out that quad-dominant and glute-dominant people use the heel differently. The quad-dominant mover sits back into the heels. For the glute-dominant mover, the heel plays a much smaller role. Watch a fascia-driven athlete take off from one leg and a quad-dominant viewer will often assume it must be a heel strike, because they can't imagine moving any other way.

He compares it to *The Matrix*. If you've never felt your glutes drive a movement, how would you know something is missing? Your body's normal is the only normal you know, until you feel something different.

## Four stages of change

Xie describes a progression he calls the **Hyperarch Metamorphosis**, based on what he has seen in his athletes:

1. **Ankle locking.** The ankle starts acting as one unit with the shin. Some people see the anterior tibial tendon pop out.
2. **First sensations in the glutes.** Occasional tingling in the glutes when you put tension through the foot, but not yet consistent.
3. **Strong glute contraction.** A clear, reliable glute response whenever tension is applied through the feet.
4. **Fully fascia-driven movement**, where the change is built in.

Behind this is his idea that the foot is **moldable**. Bend something briefly and it springs back. Apply consistent pressure over time and its shape changes. Function shapes form.

## Elasticity: the science you can lean on

Why would a tensioned, springy system make you more athletic? Here the research is strong.

- **Your arch is a spring.** A landmark 1987 study in *Nature* by Ker, Alexander and colleagues showed that the arch of the human foot stores elastic energy during running and returns it by recoil. As they put it, the runner moves "in an analogous fashion to a rubber ball bouncing along."
- **Your tendons do the bouncing.** In a 2001 ultrasound study, Fukunaga and colleagues found that during the stance phase of walking, calf muscle fibres worked almost isometrically, holding their length, while the Achilles tendon stretched and recoiled. They called this "spring-like behaviour" that stores and releases elastic energy. The muscle holds. The connective tissue springs.
- **Fascia can be trained for this.** Robert Schleip and Divo Müller's 2013 paper on fascial training principles recommends **elastic recoil**, **preparatory counter-movements**, slow and dynamic stretching, rehydration and proprioceptive refinement. They suggest training once or twice a week and expecting a more resilient "fascial body suit" over **6 to 24 months**.

That is the scientific core of what Xie calls fascial tensioning. Good tension, in his view, is what elite performance is made of. Poor tension is where problems start.

## Accuracy and movement are one thing

In his *Muscle Driven vs Fascia Driven* clip, Xie makes a bold point: in elite athletes, movement and accuracy are tied together, not separate skills. He points to athletes who excel at sports outside their own. Boxer Manny Pacquiao, for example, also played professional basketball in the Philippines.

Most training treats "skill" and "body" as different departments. Xie argues that how you are connected fascially shapes how accurate you can be. Think about it this way: many people can press the same dumbbell with each arm, yet can't throw a ball with equal power and accuracy with both. The muscles are balanced. In Xie's view, the connection is not.

This is his model, not a proven law. But it matches what every coach sees: some athletes simply look *connected*.

## Fascia as a sensory organ

There's one more reason connection matters. Fascia is rich in sensory nerve endings. Xie describes it as a superhighway for signals, which he believes helps explain why well-connected athletes learn skills faster and react quicker. Fascia researchers, including Schleip's group, describe fascial tissue as a whole-body, continuous matrix with a role in **mechanosensory fine-tuning**. How much that drives athletic skill is still an open question, and an exciting one.

## Your takeaway

You don't have to be born fascia-driven. Xie's whole message is that the spectrum is something you can travel along. The rest of this module shows you how he thinks you do it.
key_takeaways: Xie places every athlete on a spectrum from muscle-driven and quad-dominant to fascia-driven and glute-dominant.
Elite markers in his view: higher ankle stiffness, less ankle collapse, higher functional stiffness and glute dominance.
His Hyperarch Metamorphosis describes four stages, from ankle locking to strong, consistent glute response.
Strong research shows the foot arch and tendons act as springs (Ker 1987; Fukunaga 2001), and fascia-oriented training uses elastic recoil over months, not weeks (Schleip & Müller 2013).
Xie's idea that movement and accuracy are linked through fascial connection is his coaching model, not yet proven science.

lessons.title: The Weakest Link: Where Gym Culture Goes Wrong
lessons.summary: Most muscle strain injuries involve connective tissue, yet most programmes only train muscle. Chong Xie's critique of mainstream training, what he says harms fascia, and why weights still have a place.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Train the weakest link

Here is the argument in one sentence: **if most strain injuries involve connective tissue, then training only muscle means training around the weak link, not through it.**

This is where Chong Xie and mainstream research line up closely.

In 2019, sports scientist **Jan Wilke** and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis of imaging studies on lower-limb muscle strain injuries in athletes. Pooling 16 studies, they found:

- myotendinous lesions (where muscle meets tendon) in about **68%** of cases
- myofascial lesions in about **32%**
- lesions confined to the muscle tissue alone in only about **13%**

(The categories overlap, so they don't add to 100.) In other words, a "pulled hamstring" usually involves the collagen-rich connective tissue, not just the muscle fibres.

In his joint webinar with Chong Xie, Robert Schleip walks through this review and draws the obvious conclusion: if most of your strain injuries happen in the fascial system, that is your weakest link. So stop only making the muscles stronger, and train the weak link.

One honest caveat: the review found mixed evidence on whether fascial damage changes return-to-play time. The *location* finding is strong. What to do about it is still being studied.

## What Xie thinks goes wrong in the gym

In his *Crash Course*, Xie lays out his critique of muscle-focused, hypertrophy-based training. It's bold, so read it as his coaching view:

- **It reinforces segmented movement.** If your fascial connection isn't there yet, lifting trains muscles to fire in isolation instead of as one web.
- **It teaches you to drive through your heels**, which in his view conditions the wrong pattern.
- **It can make athletes robotic.** He says heavy hypertrophy work on top of poor connection often costs athletes their relaxation and flow.
- **It can widen the gap.** In a squat, he says, elite naturals use core and glutes while average lifters use quads and lower back. Same lift, different pattern. So the naturals get better and everyone else can drift the wrong way.
- **Bigger muscles don't fix chronic pain.** A smaller muscle may limit how high you jump, he argues, but it isn't what causes most chronic pain. In his view, the problem usually sits in the fascia.

## But weights are not the enemy

This matters. Xie does **not** say never lift. He says plainly that weights are not bad, and that a good coach can use proper periodization and strength work to maximise output once the fascial connections are in place.

So the message is about **order**: connection first, then load. You don't build a tall house on a cracked foundation.

## What harms your fascia

Part three of his *Crash Course* lists the factors he believes damage fascial fitness:

1. **Shoes.** Thick heel cushions, built-in arch support, narrow or raised toe boxes. He sees shoes and orthotics acting like crutches that let the foot's small muscles weaken. His fix: spend more time barefoot.
2. **Lifting on a poor connection.** As above.
3. **Mental and emotional stress**, which he believes leaves fascia tight and dehydrated.
4. **Poor sleep**, which he links to poorer overnight tissue repair.
5. **Missing nutrients**, especially vitamin C, collagen and antioxidants, which he sees as the raw materials for remodelling.

Some of this is well grounded (vitamin C is essential for collagen synthesis), and some is his clinical reasoning. Either way, this is where the **holistic** view of this course comes alive. Your fascia isn't separate from your stress, your sleep or your plate. The body pillar is connected to the others.

## Fascia is alive, and it can contract

One reason the old picture of fascia as passive wrapping is fading: research from Schleip's group has shown that fascia contains **myofibroblasts**, cells with smooth-muscle-like contractile ability. A 2019 study in *Frontiers in Physiology* found that fascial tissue contracts in response to certain stimuli, and concluded that its tension is actively regulated by these cells, with the potential to influence musculoskeletal dynamics.

The key detail: these contractions are **slow**. A 2014 review from the same group describes fascia regulating its own stiffness over **minutes to hours**, not split seconds. So fascia is not a second set of fast muscles. It is a living tissue that tunes its stiffness over time, in response to how you load it.

Xie builds on this. He describes HFT as stimulating healthy tissue remodelling without relying on breaking muscle down, which he believes is why his athletes recover quickly between sessions.

## Why this is personal

Josh lived the mainstream route: injury, physio, rest, repeat. What changed was not lifting more. It was fixing the foundation. In Josh's experience, once his fascial health was right, the injuries stopped. That's his conviction, earned the hard way, and it's the heart of this course.
key_takeaways: A 2019 meta-analysis found only about 13% of lower-limb strain injuries were confined to muscle tissue; most involved connective tissue.
Schleip's takeaway: if most injuries happen in fascia, train the weakest link, not just the strong muscles.
Xie argues muscle-only training can reinforce segmented, heel-heavy, robotic movement when fascial connection is poor.
Xie is not anti-weights: connection first, then load with good periodization.
He lists shoes, stress, poor sleep and missing nutrients as factors that harm fascia. Fascia does contract, but slowly, over minutes to hours.

lessons.title: Practice: Chong Xie's Basic Three and Ball Rolling
lessons.summary: Three barefoot exercises and one small ball. Chong Xie's free starter routine for building the foot-to-glute connection at home, with the dosing used in his published trial.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Simple on purpose

This is the part Josh loves most: no gym, no machine, no physio appointment. Chong Xie's starter routine is three barefoot exercises plus rolling with a small ball. His *Basic 3* video demonstrates them in order: Elevated Towel Curls, the HFT Swing, and the HFT Gait Cycle, followed by rolling.

Versions of these drills, elevated towel curls, single-leg balance while gripping a marble, foot-to-glute rolling and heel-to-toe movement drills, were part of the 12-week programme tested in his published 2026 trial. That programme was done barefoot, roughly three sessions a week, about 2 to 3 sets per exercise, each set lasting until fatigue or about 1 to 2 minutes of work.

Watch the demo videos before you start. Detail matters.

## Exercise 1: Elevated Towel Curls

### How to do it
- Stand on a cotton towel.
- Press down through the **ball of the foot** and lift your heel slightly off the floor. Start with a small lift and progress.
- Grab the towel with **all** your toes, little toes included, then release. Grab, release.
- Use every toe joint, not just the big toe.
- Put real weight on the working foot. This is not a seated physio drill.

### Sets and timing
Start with 2 to 3 sets per foot, working for about a minute or until the foot fatigues. Build gradually. Many beginners find even a minute surprisingly hard.

### Why it works (in Xie's view)
Keeping the heel up isolates the toes and arch, wakes up toe joints that shoes have stiffened, and activates the long tendons on top of the foot so they transfer force properly. It trains the foot to lock into the Hyperarch position, so you're more stable on one leg.

### Common mistakes
- Letting the heel drop to the floor.
- Using only the big toe, or keeping the toes straight.
- Too little weight on the foot.

Xie's self-check: people with functional glutes feel this in the glutes. People without that connection feel it mainly in the foot.

## Exercise 2: The HFT Swing (with a marble)

### How to do it
- Grip a **marble** with the toes of one foot. The grip creates tension through the sole of that foot.
- Balance on the other leg and **swing the gripping leg freely, front to back**.
- Hold a wall for balance at first if you need to. Over time, aim to balance using your foot alone.

### Sets and timing
Use the same structure: 2 to 3 sets per side, about a minute each.

### Why it works (in Xie's view)
The grip keeps tension in one foot while that leg moves freely and the standing foot works to balance you. It teaches the body to keep foot tension through motion, which is exactly what you need when you run and land.

### Common mistakes
- Dropping the marble mid-swing, which means the tension has gone.
- Stiff, forced swings. Keep it free and relaxed.
- Never progressing away from the wall.

## Exercise 3: The HFT Gait Cycle

### How to do it
Follow Xie's demo in the *Basic 3* video. The key cue is **slow and smooth**. Move through the step with control, rolling through the foot and keeping tension through the ball of the foot.

### Sets and timing
Build it into the same sessions, a few slow minutes per side.

### Why it works (in Xie's view)
Slow, smooth movement encourages fascial layers to glide. That links to real anatomy: in 2018, Carla Stecco's team in Padova identified **fasciacytes**, specialised cells in fascia that produce hyaluronan, the slippery substance that lets fascial layers slide over each other. Xie's view is that slow, loaded movement keeps that gliding system healthy.

### Common mistakes
Rushing. If it's fast, it's not this exercise.

## The tool: one small ball

In his rolling video, *You Are Foam Rolling Wrong!*, Xie explains why he prefers a tennis ball to a foam roller: the big roller is too broad for the small tissues he wants to reach.

### How to do it
- **Sole of the foot:** roll front to back, heel included, with moderate pressure until it feels warm.
- **Calves:** underneath and both sides.
- **Hips:** the side, the inside, and where the hamstring meets the hip.
- Compare left and right. Which side is more sensitive?

This follows the same foot-to-calf-to-glute path used in the trial's rolling work.

### Sets and timing
Give each area at least a couple of minutes. Fascia responds slowly to mechanical load, so a quick 30-second pass won't do much. Roll after the Basic Three to see whether tender spots are easing over the weeks.

### Common mistakes
- Rolling for 30 seconds and moving on.
- Pressing too lightly, or so hard you tense up.

## Progress, not perfection

More advanced students can add **Hyperarch hops and bounces**, keeping the ankle locked; the trial's programme progressed from two-foot to single-leg jumps. Schleip's research suggests fascia remodels over 6 to 24 months. So be patient. Josh didn't fix years of injuries in a week either. Short sessions, two or three times a week, every week, is the whole secret.

## Train smart

In the published trial, three participants stopped because of moderate problems such as increased ankle instability or knee pain, all during unsupervised sessions. The researchers suggested supervision may matter. So start gently, film yourself or train with a partner while you learn the technique, and back off if something feels wrong.

*If you have a current injury, recent surgery or ongoing pain, check with a qualified professional before starting, and stop if anything feels sharp or wrong.*
key_takeaways: Xie's starter routine: Elevated Towel Curls, the HFT Swing with a marble, and the HFT Gait Cycle, done barefoot, followed by ball rolling.
Versions of these drills were part of the programme in his 2026 randomized trial: about three sessions a week, 2-3 sets per exercise of roughly 1-2 minutes.
Towel curls: heel slightly up, weight through the ball of the foot, grip with every toe.
Gait Cycle: slow and smooth, to support fascial glide (linked to hyaluronan-producing fasciacytes, Stecco 2018).
Expect change over months, not days, and learn the technique carefully: the trial's only adverse events happened during unsupervised practice.

lessons.evidence_note: Exercise technique comes from Xie's demo videos; a multicomponent HFT programme including these drills showed positive results in one company-funded RCT (2026), but the individual exercises have not been tested in isolation.

open_questions_for_josh: Name check: the creator is Coach Chong Xie (you said 'Xiong She'). 'The Secret of Athleticism' is his website and Instagram brand (secret-of-athleticism.com, @secretofathleticism). His YouTube channel is titled 'Coach Chong Xie' (@HyperarchFasciaTraining). You also mentioned 'Athletic Freedom' as a channel name; I couldn't connect that to him. Do you want the course to say 'The Secret of Athleticism' or 'Hyperarch Fascia Training (HFT)'?

The earlier draft quoted Xie from a 'John Stockton podcast' (the 'you are not unathletic' line, 'three exercises, two to three times a week', 60% body weight on towel curls, and 'up to 40% jump gains'). I could not find any such episode. Stockton's show, The Ultimate Assist, lists no Chong Xie episode. Those quotes were removed. If you know the episode, send the link and we can restore them.

HFT is a commercial system with paid programmes and a Patreon, and its first trial was funded by the company. Are you happy featuring him this heavily, and do you want to contact him for permission, a quote or a collaboration before publishing on LinkedIn?

The HFT trial is now published (Sports, October 2026): about 46% average jump-height gain vs about 19% in controls, plus better ankle stability, but with 50% dropout in the HFT group. Are you happy with how Lesson 1 presents both the headline result and the caveats?
Which of the Basic Three do you personally do, how often, and for how long? A short 'Josh's routine' box in Lesson 5 would be powerful.
Your injury story for Lessons 1 and 4: which injuries, roughly what years, how much physio, and when you found Chong Xie's work. Please confirm your last physio visit was 2021 or 2022.
Do you agree with Xie that weights are fine once fascial connections are built? Do you still lift, and how do you combine it with fascia work?

Where would you place yourself on Xie's muscle-driven to fascia-driven spectrum, then and now? Have any of his 'elite natural' signs (prominent anterior tibial tendon, double calf, heel suspension) appeared in your own body? This could link to your movement-video breakdown.
Xie sometimes generalises about national groups and childhood environments. Following your brief, all of that is left out. Confirm you're happy to keep the course to individual athletes only.
Lesson 5 now has a short 'train smart' note (based on the trial's adverse events) and a medical-safety line. Keep, soften or remove?
